pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 3). The COMMUTATIVE property of multiplication (a×b = b×a) and the recognition that division is NOT commutative.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'show that multiplication of 2 numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of 1 number by another cannot'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.5 'apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide — e.g. if 6×4=24 is known, then 4×6=24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication)'.
• Operational details: prove commutativity with the ROTATED ARRAY (3 rows of 4 = 4 rows of 3), which both convinces and halves the fact-learning load. Equally important: teach the counterexample that division is NOT commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12) so children don't over-generalise. Use commutativity as a strategy to derive and check facts.
• Checkpoint: apply and bound the property. Tier A (6): agree 2×5 = 5×2 using a rotated array. Tier B (6–7): use commutativity to state an unknown fact from a known one (know 3×8 → 8×3). Tier C (7): explain WHY multiplication is commutative (rotate the array) and give a counterexample showing division is not.
bestPractices: Prove commutativity concretely by rotating an array a quarter turn — same objects, same total, different reading — rather than stating it as a rule; the array makes it self-evident.
Explicitly use commutativity to lighten fact learning: knowing 3×8 gives 8×3 for free, so the multiplication square is nearly halved by its diagonal symmetry.

Teach the boundary firmly: division is NOT commutative — have children test 12÷3 vs 3÷12 with counters and see they differ, so the property isn't wrongly generalised (a very common error, also later applied wrongly to subtraction).
Connect to context: 3 bags of 4 and 4 bags of 3 are different situations but the SAME product — distinguishing 'same answer' from 'same story'.
Use commutativity as a checking strategy (compute both ways, compare) to build self-correction.
keyRepresentations: The array rotated 90° (the proof of commutativity)
Paired context pictures (3 groups of 4 vs 4 groups of 3)
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising commutativity to division and subtraction (thinking 12÷3 = 3÷12, or 8−3 = 3−8).
Believing 3×4 and 4×3 are different facts needing separate memorisation.
Accepting commutativity as a stated rule without being able to justify it (no array reasoning).
Confusing 'same product' with 'same situation' — not seeing that different stories can share an answer.
Applying commutativity correctly to × but then assuming order never matters in any calculation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2; in the US this content is formally taught in Grade 3, usually ages 8–9): teach that multiplication is commutative (a×b = b×a) by rotating an array so the same objects give the same total read two ways, use this to nearly halve fact-learning, and firmly teach the boundary that division is NOT commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12) to prevent over-generalising. Learners should predict then prove commutativity by action, use it as a strategy to derive and check facts, and refute the claim that order never matters.

activities.title: Predict then rotate the array to prove 3×4 = 4×3
feedback: If you predicted the total would change, compare your prediction with what you counted — turning the array does not add or take away any objects, so the total must stay the same.
Strong answer: 'It's the same counters turned on their side, so there are still 12.' That reasons from the array, not just from working both sums out.
If a learner only says 'I worked them both out', push for the structural reason: show them the rotation so commutativity is seen, not just checked.
activities.rationale: Committing to a prediction and then proving commutativity concretely by a quarter-turn of the array makes the property self-evident and distinguishes 'same answer' from an unjustified rule; this reflects standards and mastery guidance on using the rotated array.
sourceClaims: Y2: show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of one number by another cannot.
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 counters (or dots) and count the total: 12.
Before you turn the array, predict whether the total will change if you turn it, and give your reason.
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3 — do not add or remove any counters.
Count again and confirm the total is still 12; record 3×4 = 4×3.
Repeat with another pair you choose (e.g. 2×5 and 5×2) and state the matching fact.
Explain in your own words WHY the total cannot change when you turn the array.
activities.intendedInsight: The same set of objects, read in two directions, gives the same product, so multiplication can be done in either order — this is predicted and then seen by rotating, not merely stated as a rule.

activities.title: Use commutativity to get facts for free
feedback: If a learner recomputes the partner fact, remind them the array proof means the answer must be identical — they already know it.
Encourage them to point to the diagonal mirror on the square to justify why the facts pair up.
Note the facts that sit on the diagonal (like 3×3) have no separate partner, which is why commutativity nearly halves, rather than exactly halves, the facts to learn.
activities.rationale: Explicitly using commutativity as a strategy lightens fact learning and supports self-correction, as highlighted in the standards and mastery guidance.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.5 apply the commutative property of multiplication as a strategy (know 6×4=24 → 4×6=24).
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Given a known fact (e.g. 3×8 = 24), state its commuted partner (8×3 = 24) without recomputing.
Look at a multiplication square and find the diagonal line of symmetry; notice that facts on either side of it mirror each other.
Decide which of a pair is easier to work out (e.g. 2×9 vs 9×2) and explain why using the easier order helps.
Use 'compute both ways and compare' to check one of your own answers.
activities.intendedInsight: Because order doesn't matter for multiplication, each known fact gives its partner free, nearly halving the facts to learn, and you can pick the easier order or check your work.

activities.title: Test the boundary: division does not swap
feedback: If a learner says 12÷3 = 3÷12 'because order doesn't matter in maths', have them physically share both ways; the different outcomes make the difference felt.
Good distinction: '12÷3 gives 4, but 3÷12 gives less than one — division can't be turned round.'
Note that subtraction also does not commute (8−3 ≠ 3−8), so 'order never matters' is the mistaken rule to avoid.
activities.rationale: Teaching the counterexample firmly heads off the very common over-generalisation of commutativity to division and subtraction, which the curriculum and mastery guidance call out explicitly.
sourceClaims: Y2: show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of one number by another cannot.
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Act out 12 ÷ 3 with counters: share 12 counters into 3 equal groups and count one group (4).
Now act out 3 ÷ 12: try to share 3 counters among 12 — you cannot give everyone a whole counter, so each would get less than one.
Compare the two results and state clearly that 12÷3 ≠ 3÷12 (4 is not the same as less than one).
Try to 'rotate' the sharing the way you rotated a multiplication array, and describe why it does not work.
Decide for each pair whether order can swap: sort statements (mixing × and ÷) into 'order can swap' and 'order matters'.
Consider whether swapping works for subtraction too (e.g. 8−3 vs 3−8) and say what you find.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication's array can be turned freely without changing the total, but swapping the two numbers in a division (or subtraction) usually changes the answer (it only stays the same when the two numbers are equal) — so the swapping shortcut has a precise stopping point.

activities.title: Same product, different story
feedback: If a learner thinks the stories must be identical because the totals match, point to the different group sizes — 3 bags of 4 is a different arrangement from 4 bags of 3.
If a learner thinks the totals differ because the stories differ, have them count both to 12.
activities.rationale: Connecting commutativity to context distinguishes 'same product' from 'same situation', addressing a listed misconception.
learnerActions: Draw or set out '3 bags of 4' and '4 bags of 3' as two separate situations.
Confirm both give 12, then explain how the stories differ even though the answer is the same.
Match a context picture to the fact it shows, and to its commuted partner.
activities.intendedInsight: Different real situations can share the same product; 'same answer' is not the same as 'same story'.

activities.title: Refute the character who says division swaps too
feedback: A convincing refutation does the sharing: 12 shared into 3 is 4 each, but 3 shared among 12 is less than one.
If the learner just says 'no' without evidence, ask them to show it with counters.
activities.rationale: A character over-generalising invites Socratic refutation; the disproof is more convincing when the learner manipulates quantities and produces a worked counterexample rather than merely asserting, so this works as a supplement to hands-on testing.
learnerActions: Listen to a character claim 'division works both ways, like multiplication — 12÷3 is the same as 3÷12'.
Disagree and give a counterexample, backing it up by sharing counters both ways.
State the correct rule: multiplication can be swapped, division cannot.
activities.intendedInsight: You can justify and defend the boundary of commutativity by producing a worked counterexample, not just asserting it.

constraints: Prove commutativity by action (rotating the array) rather than stating it as a rule; a static paired image or captioned diagram is a useful reference but cannot itself let the learner perform the rotation or test the division counterexample.
Always teach the division (and subtraction) boundary alongside commutativity so learners do not over-generalise 'order doesn't matter'.
True/false, matching and sort tasks check whether the learner holds the property and its boundary, but do not by themselves elicit the structural proof-by-rotation; pair them with hands-on building.

The dialogue/character task is a supplement: the actual disproof should be done by sharing quantities, not by bare assertion alone — a worked counterexample is valid reasoning; an unsupported 'no' is not.
Distinguish 'same product' from 'same situation': commutativity gives the same total, not the same story.
A learner who gets both facts right numerically but justifies only by 'I worked them both out' has not yet reached the structural insight; prompt for the array reason.
Commutativity nearly halves (not exactly halves) the facts to learn, because facts on the diagonal of the multiplication square (e.g. 3×3) have no separate partner.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Of the cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified in the row; the CCSS 3.OA.5 and NCETM claims are marked unverified. Do not treat them as confirmed.
Arithmetic checked: 3×4=12 and 4×3=12; 3×5=15 and 5×3=15; 3×8=24 and 8×3=24; 2×9=18 and 9×2=18; 12÷3=4; 3÷12=0.25 (<1); 8−3=5 and 3−8=−5; these are consistent across the activities.

Acting out 3÷12 yields a fractional result (1/4) that sits beyond typical Y2 scope and is awkward with whole counters; it is preserved from the original assessment and used only as an observable 'each gets less than one' contrast, not as formal fraction work.

The original Predict–Observe–Explain assessment task (predict 'more/fewer/same' and why, then build and count) has been reintegrated into Activity 1 as a prediction step so the discriminating commitment is not lost.

The original noted a 3D interactive 'adds nothing conceptual'; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been omitted rather than asserted as a universal law. Planar rotation is sufficient to show the proof, which is retained as a scoped point.

assess.poeTask: Set out 3 groups of 5 counters. Before building the comparison, ask the child to PREDICT: 'If I make 5 groups of 3 instead, will the total be more, fewer, or the same — and why?' They commit to a reason, then build 5 groups of 3 and count. Predicting 'the same' with a rotate/rearrange reason shows commutative understanding; predicting 'different' reveals the order-changes-the-total misconception.
probeDeeper: Show me with an array why 3 × 5 = 5 × 3.
Which is easier to work out, 2 × 9 or 9 × 2? Why does that help?
Draw 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 — do they look the same?
Does swapping work for adding? For subtracting?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 (both 15) — it's the same array turned on its side, so multiplication can be done in either order. But 12 ÷ 3 (= 4) is NOT the same as 3 ÷ 12 (less than one) — division can't be swapped round.

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises commutativity to division — thinks 12 ÷ 3 = 3 ÷ 12 because 'order doesn't matter in maths'
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out 12 ÷ 3 (4 each) versus 3 ÷ 12 (sharing 3 among 12) with counters so the difference is felt; contrast with the rotate-the-array move for ×
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says division can be swapped just like multiplication

errorPatterns.pattern: denies 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 — thinks '3 groups of 5' and '5 groups of 3' give different totals because the order changes the meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: build both sets, count each to 15, then rotate one array onto the other to show the total is identical
errorPatterns.distractor: No, 3 groups of 5 is different from 5 groups of 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: accepts 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 numerically but has no structural reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: rotate a 3 × 5 array to 5 × 3 — same counters, same total — so commutativity is seen, not merely checked
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct answer justified only by 'I worked them both out'

responseLevels.gap: Thinks multiplication order changes the total, or swaps division freely.
responseLevels.full: Explains multiplication commutes using a rotated array, uses it to pick the easier calculation, and shows division does not commute.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 (and that division differs) but justifies only by computing, not by the array structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 3 × 5 the same as 5 × 3? And is 12 ÷ 3 the same as 3 ÷ 12? For each one, tell me yes or no and how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pairing × (which commutes) with ÷ (which doesn't) tests whether the child has a REASON — the rotated array, the different meanings of ÷ — rather than an over-general rule 'order doesn't matter'. A child who swaps both has a rule without understanding; one who only checks numerically misses the structural insight.
